title: Usha and JD Vance Welcome Son Alec Neel, First Baby Born to a Sitting VP in 156 Years
excerpt: The Indian-American second lady gave birth at Walter Reed Medical Center on Sunday, making history as the first VP spouse to have a child in office since 1870.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Usha and JD Vance welcomed their fourth child, Alec Neel, at Walter Reed Medical Center.
  • Alec is the first baby born to a sitting vice president since 1870, a gap of 156 years.
  • Usha Vance is the highest-ranking Indian-American woman in the executive branch.
  • Alec joins siblings Ewan, Vivek, and Mirabel, and is the third child of Trump officials this year.
Historic Birth in the Vice Presidency
›First child born to a sitting VP since 1870.
›Previous record held by Schuyler Colfax III.
›156 years between births of VP children.
›John C. Calhoun's son born in 1829.
  • Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance welcomed their fourth child, Alec Neel Vance, at Walter Reed Medical Center on Sunday.
  • The birth makes history — Alec is the first baby born to a sitting vice president since Schuyler Colfax III in 1870, a gap of 156 years.
  • Usha Vance, née Chilukuri, is the daughter of Indian immigrants and the highest-ranking Indian-American woman in the executive branch.
  • The baby joins siblings Ewan, 9, Vivek, 6, and Mirabel, 4, and is the third child born to Trump administration officials this year.

Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance announced on Sunday the birth of their fourth child, a boy named Alec Neel Vance, at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland.

"We are excited to announce that our baby boy, Alec Neel Vance, was born this morning," the couple said in a statement posted on X. "Usha and the baby are happy and healthy, and our kids are overjoyed to meet their little brother."

A Historic First in 156 Years

Alec's arrival carries a distinction no living American can claim: he is the first child born to a sitting vice president since 1870, when Schuyler Colfax III was born during Ulysses S. Grant's first term. Before that, John C. Calhoun's son William was born in 1829 while Calhoun served as Andrew Jackson's vice president, according to the White House Historical Association.

> **"The vice president jokingly praised Usha's frugality after the dress controversy, writing on social media: "She bought a $50 dress for $8.75."**

"The vice president jokingly praised Usha's frugality after the dress controversy, writing on social media: "She bought a $50 dress for $8.75."

The Vances thanked "the incredible military doctors and staff members of Walter Reed Medical Center and the White House Medical Unit" for their care. Alec joins older siblings Ewan, 9, Vivek, 6, and Mirabel, 4.

"We are excited to announce that our baby boy, Alec Neel Vance, was born this morning. Usha and the baby are happy and healthy, and our kids are overjoyed to meet their little brother."

— JD and Usha Vance, in a statement on X

The Indian-American Second Lady

Usha Vance, 40, née Chilukuri, is the daughter of immigrants from the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh. A former attorney who clerked for Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts and then-Circuit Judge Brett Kavanaugh, she met JD Vance at Yale Law School, where both graduated in 2013. She also hosts "Storytime with the Second Lady," a podcast on Spotify and YouTube launched during her pregnancy.

Her pregnancy, announced in January 2026, drew intense public attention. The New York Times' fashion critic noted that the maternity style of Vance, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, and deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller's wife Katie Miller offered "an image of idealized womanhood that gives literal shape to the pronatalist movement." Usha Vance responded with characteristic dry humor, revealing the dress in question was an $8.75 coral maternity dress from Old Navy.

Usha Vance: A Trailblazer
›Daughter of Indian immigrants from Andhra Pradesh.
›First Indian-American second lady in U.S. history.
›Hosts 'Storytime with the Second Lady' podcast.
›Graduated from Yale Law School in 2013.

Why the Decision to Have a Fourth Child

Vice President Vance, 41, has long been an advocate for larger families and has expressed alarm about declining birth rates. In his recent memoir, he wrote that the September 2025 assassination of conservative activist and friend Charlie Kirk influenced the family's decision. Erika Kirk, Charlie's widow, told the Vances she wished she had more than two children with her husband.

In a CBS Sunday Morning interview in June, Usha Vance offered a more nuanced take: "It was very powerful, what [Erika] said about her own family, and certainly very moving to both of us. I think I had already started to open my mind to the possibility. I wouldn't say that this was, for me in any way, the decisive factor. But it came in the middle of a conversation that we were already having."

A Baby Boom in the White House

Alec is the third child born to senior Trump administration officials in 2026. Karoline Leavitt welcomed her second child with husband Nicholas Riccio in May, and Katie Miller, wife of deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, recently had the couple's fourth child. The vice president jokingly praised Usha's frugality after the dress controversy, writing on social media: "She bought a $50 dress for $8.75. America: meet your next director of the federal budget!"

A Baby Boom in the White House
›Alec is the third child of Trump officials in 2026.
›Karoline Leavitt's second child born in May 2026.
›Katie Miller's fourth child also born in 2026.
›Usha's frugality highlighted in social media post.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian-American community, Usha Vance's role as second lady — and now as a mother of four in the White House — represents the community's deepening footprint in American public life. She is the first Indian-American to serve as second lady, following Vice President Kamala Harris, who was the first person of Indian descent to hold either of the two highest offices. The choice of middle name Neel, which has roots in Sanskrit, also resonated with the diaspora on social media.
